units.title: The United States on the Map
units.blurb: Where the country is, its 50 states and capital, its territories, its regions and the two-letter postal codes.

units.title: States and Capitals by Region
units.blurb: Every state and its capital, region by region, then all fifty together, and which states share a border.

units.title: Land and Water
units.blurb: The physical regions, mountain ranges, high and low points, rivers, the Great Lakes, coasts, deserts, Alaska and Hawaii.

units.title: National Parks and Landmarks
units.blurb: What a national park is, famous parks of the West and the East, and landmarks you can find on the map.

units.title: Time Zones and Climate
units.blurb: Why clocks differ across the country, how to figure the time somewhere else, and the main climate regions.

units.title: People and Places
units.blurb: Where Americans live, the largest cities, the most and least populous states, and what grows and is made where.

units.title: How the Country Grew
units.blurb: The first thirteen states, the lands the country added, and the order in which states joined, as dated facts.

topics.title: Where Is the United States?
topics.short: The United States is in North America, between Canada and Mexico, with the Atlantic Ocean to the east and the Pacific to the west.
topics.trouble: Students think Alaska is an island near Mexico because many maps put it in a small box in the corner. Alaska is in the far northwest, next to Canada.

topics.title: Fifty States and a Capital
topics.short: The country has 50 states and the District of Columbia; 48 states touch one another, and Alaska and Hawaii stand apart.
topics.trouble: Students think Washington, D.C., is in Washington State, or that it is a state. The District of Columbia is a federal district on the East Coast, between Maryland and Virginia.

topics.title: U.S. Territories
topics.short: Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa are U.S. territories, not states.
topics.trouble: Students think Puerto Rico is a separate country or a state. It is a U.S. territory, and people born there are U.S. citizens.

topics.title: Regions of the United States
topics.short: The U.S. Census Bureau groups the states into four regions: the Northeast, the Midwest, the South and the West.
topics.trouble: Students expect one official way to divide the country. Many books use five regions (adding a Southeast and a Southwest); this ladder uses the Census Bureau's four regions and nine divisions.

topics.title: State Postal Codes
topics.short: Each state has a two-letter postal code, such as CA for California, TX for Texas and NY for New York.
topics.trouble: Students guess from the first two letters: AK is Alaska and AR is Arkansas; MI is Michigan, MN Minnesota, MS Mississippi, MO Missouri, MA Massachusetts, ME Maine and MD Maryland.

topics.title: States of the Northeast
topics.short: Find the nine states of the Northeast: the six New England states and New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the small New England states, especially Vermont and New Hampshire (Vermont is the western one, New Hampshire touches the ocean).

topics.title: Capitals of the Northeast
topics.short: Match each Northeastern state with its capital, such as Albany for New York and Boston for Massachusetts.
topics.trouble: Students pick the biggest city: New York's capital is Albany, not New York City, and Pennsylvania's is Harrisburg, not Philadelphia.

topics.title: States of the Midwest
topics.short: Find the twelve Midwestern states, from Ohio in the east to North Dakota, Nebraska and Kansas in the west.
topics.trouble: Students switch Iowa and Missouri, or Nebraska and Kansas (Nebraska is the northern one, Kansas is directly south of it).

topics.title: Capitals of the Midwest
topics.short: Match each Midwestern state with its capital, such as Springfield for Illinois and Saint Paul for Minnesota.
topics.trouble: Students pick the biggest city: Illinois's capital is Springfield, not Chicago; Michigan's is Lansing, not Detroit; Missouri's is Jefferson City.

topics.title: States of the South Atlantic
topics.short: Find the South Atlantic states, from Delaware and Maryland down the coast to Florida, plus West Virginia and Washington, D.C.
topics.trouble: Students forget that Delaware, Maryland and West Virginia count as part of the South in the Census Bureau's regions.

topics.title: Capitals of the South Atlantic
topics.short: Match each South Atlantic state with its capital, such as Tallahassee for Florida and Raleigh for North Carolina.
topics.trouble: Students pick Miami for Florida or Charlotte for North Carolina; the capitals are Tallahassee and Raleigh.

topics.title: States of the South Central
topics.short: Find the eight South Central states: Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama and Mississippi, and Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas.
topics.trouble: Students switch Alabama and Mississippi, which sit side by side (Mississippi is the western one, along the Mississippi River).

topics.title: Capitals of the South Central
topics.short: Match each South Central state with its capital, such as Austin for Texas and Nashville for Tennessee.
topics.trouble: Students pick Houston for Texas or New Orleans for Louisiana; the capitals are Austin and Baton Rouge.

topics.title: States of the Mountain West
topics.short: Find the eight Mountain states: Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico.
topics.trouble: Students switch Wyoming and Colorado, two near-rectangles (Wyoming is the northern one), or Arizona and New Mexico (Arizona is the western one).

topics.title: Capitals of the Mountain West
topics.short: Match each Mountain state with its capital, such as Denver for Colorado and Carson City for Nevada.
topics.trouble: Students pick Las Vegas for Nevada or Albuquerque for New Mexico; the capitals are Carson City and Santa Fe.

topics.title: States of the Pacific
topics.short: Find the five Pacific states: Washington, Oregon, California, Alaska and Hawaii.
topics.trouble: Students mix up Washington State with Washington, D.C., which is on the other side of the country.

topics.title: Capitals of the Pacific
topics.short: Match each Pacific state with its capital, such as Sacramento for California and Juneau for Alaska.
topics.trouble: Students pick Los Angeles for California or Seattle for Washington; the capitals are Sacramento and Olympia.

topics.title: All Fifty States
topics.short: Find any state on the map of the whole country, and name a state from its place or its shape.
topics.trouble: Students know states only inside their region and lose them on the full map; small Eastern states and the square Western states are the usual mix-ups.

topics.title: All Fifty Capitals
topics.short: Name the capital of any state, or the state that a capital belongs to.
topics.trouble: Students mix up capitals with similar names: Columbia (South Carolina) and Columbus (Ohio), Charleston (West Virginia's capital; also a big city in South Carolina), Jackson and Jefferson City.

topics.title: Neighboring States
topics.short: Name the states that share a border with a state; Tennessee and Missouri each touch eight others, and Maine touches only one.
topics.trouble: Students count states that only meet at a point: at the Four Corners, Arizona and Colorado, and Utah and New Mexico, touch only at one spot and do not share a border.

topics.title: Landform Regions
topics.short: From east to west: the Coastal Plain, the Appalachian Mountains, the Central Lowland, the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the high basins and plateaus, and the Pacific mountains.
topics.trouble: Students think the land rises evenly from east to west. The Appalachians are old, worn-down mountains in the East; the higher, younger Rockies rise suddenly at the western edge of the Great Plains.

topics.title: Mountain Ranges
topics.short: The Appalachians run near the East Coast; the Rockies run from New Mexico to Montana and on into Canada; the Sierra Nevada and the Cascades rise near the Pacific.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the Sierra Nevada (in California and Nevada) with the Rockies, or put the Appalachians in the West.

topics.title: Highest and Lowest Places
topics.short: Denali in Alaska is the highest peak in North America (20,310 feet); Badwater Basin in Death Valley is the lowest point (282 feet below sea level).
topics.trouble: Students think the highest point is in the Rockies. Denali is in the Alaska Range; the highest peak in the 48 states next to each other is Mount Whitney in California's Sierra Nevada. Denali's federal name has been Mount McKinley since 2025; Alaska and many others still call it Denali.

topics.title: The Continental Divide
topics.short: Along the high Rockies runs the Continental Divide: rain on its west side flows toward the Pacific, rain on its east side toward the Atlantic and the Gulf.
topics.trouble: Students think rivers flow toward the nearest ocean. A river flows downhill, so which side of the Divide it starts on decides where it goes.

topics.title: Major Rivers
topics.short: Find the Mississippi, Missouri, Ohio, Colorado, Columbia and Rio Grande rivers and the states they pass through.
topics.trouble: Students think the Mississippi is the longest U.S. river; by the U.S. Geological Survey's measure the Missouri is a little longer, and it flows into the Mississippi.

topics.title: The Mississippi River System
topics.short: The Missouri, Ohio and Arkansas rivers flow into the Mississippi, and the Tennessee flows into the Ohio; the Mississippi carries all their water to the Gulf.
topics.trouble: Students think a river's basin is just the river. The Mississippi's basin is all the land its tributaries drain: parts of 31 states and two Canadian provinces.

topics.title: The Great Lakes
topics.short: The five Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario ("HOMES"); Lake Michigan is the only one entirely inside the United States.
topics.trouble: Students think the Great Lakes are all in the United States. Canada shares four of them; only Lake Michigan lies wholly in the U.S.

topics.title: Coasts, Bays and Peninsulas
topics.short: Find the Atlantic, Gulf and Pacific coasts, Chesapeake Bay, Cape Cod, the Florida Peninsula, Puget Sound and San Francisco Bay.
topics.trouble: Students forget the Gulf coast, the long southern shore from Florida to Texas. Its body of water is the Gulf of Mexico; since 2025 the U.S. federal government calls it the Gulf of America.

topics.title: Deserts of the United States
topics.short: The four big deserts are the Mojave, the Sonoran, the Chihuahuan and the Great Basin, all in the West and Southwest.
topics.trouble: Students think deserts are only hot. The Great Basin Desert is a cold desert, with snowy winters.

topics.title: Alaska and Hawaii
topics.short: Alaska is the largest state, with glaciers, mountains and tundra; Hawaii is a chain of volcanic islands in the middle of the Pacific.
topics.trouble: Students judge Alaska's size from small inset maps. Alaska is more than twice as big as Texas.

topics.title: What Is a National Park?
topics.short: National parks protect special places for everyone; Yellowstone (1872) was the first, and the National Park Service has run the parks since 1916.
topics.trouble: Students think every park is a national park. The country has more than 60 national parks and hundreds of other places, such as monuments and historic sites, that the Park Service cares for.

topics.title: National Parks of the West
topics.short: Find Yellowstone, Yosemite, the Grand Canyon, Zion, Glacier, Rocky Mountain, Olympic, Denali and other parks of the West.
topics.trouble: Students put the Grand Canyon in Colorado because the Colorado River carved it. Grand Canyon National Park is in Arizona.

topics.title: National Parks of the Middle and East
topics.short: Find the Great Smoky Mountains, Acadia, the Everglades, Shenandoah, Mammoth Cave, Big Bend and other parks east of the Rockies.
topics.trouble: Students think all the big parks are in the West. The most visited national park is the Great Smoky Mountains, on the border of Tennessee and North Carolina.

topics.title: Famous Landmarks
topics.short: Match landmarks to their states: the Statue of Liberty (New York), Mount Rushmore (South Dakota), the Golden Gate Bridge (California), the Gateway Arch (Missouri).
topics.trouble: Students confuse landmarks made by people with natural ones. Mount Rushmore is carved by people into a natural mountain; Old Faithful is a natural geyser.

topics.title: U.S. Time Zones
topics.short: The 50 states span six time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific, Alaska and Hawaii-Aleutian; it gets earlier as you go west.
topics.trouble: Students think it is later in the West. The Sun rises first in the East, so when it is noon in New York it is 9 a.m. in California.

topics.title: What Time Is It There?
topics.short: Count the zones between two places and add hours going east or subtract going west.
topics.trouble: Students add when they should subtract. Going west, clocks are earlier: subtract one hour for each zone you cross.

topics.title: Daylight Saving Time
topics.short: In most states, clocks move ahead an hour in spring and back in fall; Hawaii and most of Arizona stay on standard time all year.
topics.trouble: Students think every state changes its clocks. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not, so in summer Arizona has the same clock time as California.

topics.title: Climate Regions
topics.short: Hot, humid summers in the Southeast; cold winters in the North; dry lands in the Southwest; mild, rainy winters on the Pacific coast; tropical Hawaii; cold Alaska.
topics.trouble: Students think the farther south, the hotter, always. Mountains and oceans matter too: coastal San Francisco has cool summers, and high Denver is colder than low places at the same latitude.

topics.title: Where Storms Strike
topics.short: Hurricanes strike the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, tornadoes are most common on the Great Plains and in the South, and earthquakes are most common in the West and Alaska.
topics.trouble: Students think tornadoes happen only in one "Tornado Alley." Tornadoes occur in every state; they are most frequent in the central and southern plains and the Southeast.

topics.title: The Largest Cities
topics.short: New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and Phoenix are the largest U.S. cities by population (2020 Census).
topics.trouble: Students think a state's largest city is its capital. Of the ten largest cities in the 2020 Census, only Phoenix is a state capital.

topics.title: Most and Fewest People
topics.short: California, Texas, Florida, New York and Pennsylvania have the most people; Wyoming has the fewest (2020 Census).
topics.trouble: Students think the biggest states by area have the most people. Alaska is the largest state but has one of the smallest populations.

topics.title: Crowded and Uncrowded
topics.short: Population density is people per square mile: New Jersey is the most crowded state and Alaska the least.
topics.trouble: Students compare total population when the question is about crowding. Density divides people by land area, so a small state can be more crowded than a big one.

topics.title: What Grows Where
topics.short: Iowa and Illinois lead in corn, Kansas and North Dakota in wheat, Texas in cotton, Idaho in potatoes, and California in fruits and vegetables.
topics.trouble: Students think one state grows everything. Crops follow climate and soil: corn needs warm, wet summers; wheat grows on the drier plains; citrus needs mild winters.

topics.title: The First Thirteen States
topics.short: The thirteen original states were the colonies along the Atlantic coast; Delaware was the first to approve the Constitution, in 1787.
topics.trouble: Students include Vermont or Maine, which were part of the land but joined as separate states later (1791 and 1820).

topics.title: Land Added to the Country
topics.short: The Louisiana Purchase (1803), Florida (1819), Texas (1845), the Oregon Country (1846), the Mexican Cession (1848), Alaska (1867) and Hawaii (1898).
topics.trouble: Students think the country simply grew westward one strip at a time. It grew by purchases, treaties, annexations and a war, in big pieces, and not always from east to west (Alaska came before many Western states).

topics.title: When the States Joined
topics.short: Put states in order of joining: Delaware first (1787) and Hawaii last (1959); many Western states joined around 1890.
topics.trouble: Students think states joined from east to west in order. Texas and California joined years before nearby states, and Alaska and Hawaii joined last, both in 1959.
